findings.evidence: uploadAudio() originally deleted the old audio asset (storage+DB) before uploading/attaching the new one inside a single @Transactional method, risking a broken audioAssetId reference if the new upload failed after the old delete succeeded.
findings.why_it_matters: A failed re-upload could leave a published Listening/Speaking question pointing at a deleted asset, breaking playback with no obvious recovery path.
findings.required_action: Remove the outer @Transactional; upload and attach the new asset first, only delete the old asset after the question is durably saved with the new audioAssetId.

findings.evidence: MIME type validation relies on the client-supplied MultipartFile.getContentType(), which is spoofable; no server-side content sniffing of the actual audio bytes.
findings.why_it_matters: A malicious upload could bypass the MIME whitelist by spoofing the Content-Type header, though the existing StorageService has no content-sniffing capability to build on.
findings.required_action: Out of scope for this phase — deeper content-type verification would require extending StorageService/CloudinaryServiceImpl itself, not just the caller.
